Pool Service in Peoria, AZ, From the Older South End to the Newest Northern Builds

Peoria runs a long way north from its older neighborhoods, and its pools range from decades old to brand new. Call the free line any hour to be put through to an independent, locally owned pool service company that works in Peoria.

Pool service in Peoria, AZ covers two very different kinds of backyard. In the older south end, pools may be on their second pump and their second coat of plaster. Up north, master-planned communities are still filling in, and many pools there are only a few years old. This page covers what each one tends to need, and how a single phone call gets a Peoria pool company on the line.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro is a phone line, not a pool company. Ring (623) 240-0428; a recorded assistant notes the trouble and your part of Peoria before passing the call to an independent, locally owned pool service company. That company looks at the pool, prices the job and does it, and you pay it, not the line.

Peoria: a city that keeps building north

Peoria stretches far to the north of its original town site, and much of its newer housing is in the north. Water planning there has followed that growth. Since the late 1990s, Peoria and Glendale have shared Colorado River water from the Central Arizona Project, and they jointly own the Pyramid Peak water treatment plant in north Phoenix. Glendale holds the larger share and operates it. The plant serves the northern parts of both cities, including Peoria's Vistancia area.

As new neighborhoods kept coming, the city looked to expand the plant to keep pace with residential growth. For a pool owner, that history means your tap water depends on where you live. The city's water FAQ shows how much that matters: water from its Greenway treatment plant averages about 13 grains per gallon of hardness, Pyramid Peak water averages about 17, and its groundwater wells run lower, at 2 to 8 grains. Peoria's yearly water quality report lists the sources and hardness for the system, and it is worth reading before anyone tells you how hard your water is.

Services Peoria pool owners ask about

Steady weekly pool cleaning and maintenance is the most common call. Owners of older pools tend to ask about pool pump repair and, once the plaster gets rough or stained, pool resurfacing. Owners of newer pools with salt systems, automation and heaters often need pool equipment repair sorted out by someone who can trace a fault through the whole pad.

An older Peoria pool and a newer one need different things

The same street rules apply to both: hard water, high heat and summer dust. What wears out first is different.

Older pools in the south end

Expect worn plaster, tile with years of scale on it, and equipment that has been patched more than once. A careful pool technician will look at the age of the pump and filter before suggesting another repair, and will tell you if the surface is near the point where repair or resurfacing is the real question.

Newer pools up north

New plaster needs careful water balance while it cures, and newer pads often carry salt cells, variable-speed pumps and automation. Keep the builder's paperwork handy. A fault in the first years may still be covered, so check that paperwork first, before any money changes hands.

Pool service in Peoria, AZ: what to ask before you agree to a plan

Every company sets its own plan and price, and the line does not quote either. These questions make two quotes easier to compare.

  • What does each weekly visit include? Skimming, brushing, vacuuming, baskets and water testing are the core. Ask how often the filter gets cleaned.
  • Do you test calcium hardness and stabilizer? Cyanuric acid (stabilizer) shields chlorine from the sun, but too much of it slows chlorine down. Both numbers matter in the desert.
  • Are chemicals in the monthly price or billed separately? Get the answer in writing.
  • What is your Arizona ROC license number? Needed for repair, equipment and resurfacing work. Look it up yourself.
  • Does my HOA have rules that affect the job? If you live in a master-planned community, check its rules on equipment changes, noise or where water may drain, and share them.

Safe checks before you call

  • Listen to the pump. Humming without spinning, grinding or screeching are all worth describing on the call. Turn it off if it is screeching.
  • Look at the pad. Note any drip or puddle at the pump, filter or heater, and clear leaves and debris away from the equipment.
  • Check the automation. A schedule can reset after an outage. Make sure the pump is set to run.
  • Test the water. A home test kit reading for chlorine and pH helps the company know what it is walking into.

Safety first. Never mix pool chemicals with each other, and keep them stored apart, dry, shaded and away from children. Do not open up motors or wiring. If a breaker trips a second time, leave it off. Never leave a child alone near the water, and keep a gate or cover on a pool that is not fenced.

Check the license first. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) licenses contractors, and its residential classifications include R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair. Repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing generally call for a licensed contractor; whether a cleaning-only service needs a license is not spelled out, so ask the ROC if it matters to you. Ask the company for its ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search (opens in a new tab) before work begins. The line does not check this for you.

Common questions

Who can I call for pool service in Peoria, AZ?

Use the free line at any hour. A recorded assistant notes the pool trouble and roughly where in Peoria you live, then connects you with an independent, locally owned pool service company. The quote, the work and the bill all come from that company.

Where does Peoria's tap water come from?

Peoria uses Colorado River water from the Central Arizona Project along with other supplies. Since the late 1990s it has shared CAP water with Glendale, and the two cities jointly own the Pyramid Peak treatment plant, which serves northern Peoria, including Vistancia. The city's water FAQ puts average hardness at about 13 grains per gallon for its Greenway plant, about 17 for Pyramid Peak and 2 to 8 for its wells, so the answer depends on which supply reaches your street.

My pool is only a few years old. Why does it need regular service?

A new pool still loses water to sun and heat, gets topped off with hard tap water and collects desert dust. Without steady testing and brushing, scale and algae can start early. Weekly care also gives someone a regular look at the equipment while any builder or manufacturer warranty may still apply.

Should I fix or replace an old pool pump in an older Peoria home?

The answer turns on which part gave out and the pump's age. A seal or a capacitor on a younger pump is often a repair. A worn-out motor on an old single-speed pump can tip the decision toward a new variable-speed pump. Ask the company for both options in writing, and see the pool pump repair page.
